I reread all the Harry Potter books last year. They are far more annoying than I remembered them to be.

Rowling is an author who seems totally obsessed with food, since she pretty much lists each item anyone ever eats for basically no reason at all. If Ron's telling Hermione something important over dinner I don't care in the slightest whether he's stuffing his face with mashed potatoes or steak and kidney pudding. It doesn't add anything.

I kind of want to cross things out in red pen and mark it "irrelevant" and send it back to her. Just tell me the story and shut up about treacle sponge unless the treacle sponge is in some way relevant (spoiler: it isn't).

The classic of course is Enid Blyton. Her children are continually hungry despite gorging themselves constantly and the food consumed is often listed despite it having nothing to do with the story.

It's one of my pet hates in writing, to be honest - those utterly unimportant but lovingly described details. I think that if a description of anything doesn't help define a character, or strengthen a world/setting, or progress the plot, it should be ruthlessly edited out.

But yeah, I reckon the majority of Sentinels heroes would end up in Gryffindor because that's where the people who aren't evil, pathetic, or clever-to-the-exclusion-of-everything-else live. Few of the characters from non-Gryffindor houses are allowed to be anything other than stereotypes of their houses.

posts.name: Ameena
posts.cooked:
Harry didn't get a lot of food as a kid - of course he's gonna be thinking about it more once he finally gets to eat whatever he likes at Hogwarts and the books are entirely from his PoV other than the occasional chapter here and there over the course of the series ;).

Also, just because someone isn't very nice doesn't mean they're automatically a Slytherin. The main characteristic of people in that House is ambition, and I'm sure there are plenty of heroes who want to make themselves better (though not necessarily at the cost of others ;)). I once saw descriptions of each House which said that Gryffindors are extroverts ruled by their hearts, Slytherins are extroverts ruled by their heads, Hufflepuffs are introverts ruled by their hearts and Ravenclaws are introverts ruled by their heads.

But ultimately it's the choice of the individual that matters - Hermione was nearly a Ravenclaw, it turns out, and anyone who's read the first book knows that Harry would probably have been a Slytherin if he hadn't asked the Hat not to put him there...though in that case it's possible that the Slytherin thing was due to some...interference. But anyway...I'm not sure I know enough about the specifics of the various Sentinels personalities to determine where they'd go, but Legacy has to be a Gryffindor, surely :D.

Nice description!

My young daughter read the books, then took the Sorting Hat test on the Pottermore site and ended up in Slytherin.  This upset her becasue they're the "bad guy" house, becuase the books are written entirely from Harry's perspective.  I explained to her that being in Slytherin just means you're ambitios and want to leave a lasting mark on the world, not that you're evil.  The books do have a few heroic Slytherins and villianous Gryffindors, not to mention brave Hufflepuffs and dimwitted Ravenclaws. The house relects one part of a character's personality, not all of it.

But yeah, the books have a serious Gryffindor bias.  Gryffindors are brave and noble, but tend not to things through. If Harry had been in Hufflepuff or Ravenclaw, he probably would've consulted with the Professors when bad things started to happen instead of keeping secrets and trying to fix everything himself.  Things might've gone better that way, but it would've made for less interesting stories.

Well I could be misremembering, but apart from pumpkin juice (there's a reason why we don't drink this in the real world) pretty much everything is ordinary unremarkable stereotypically boring British food. It makes the setting seem more mundane, not less. It's like extreme Muggle food, which never really sat well with me. Those house elves could make anything, and if you're cooking via magic you'd think wizards could be a little more adventurous than the ubiquitous meat, potatoes and two veg followed by steamed pudding. Show me that someone's complaining about the lack of vegetables, or is vegetarian, or has a phobia of gravy, or whatever, if it's telling me something about the character or the world.

Rowling's fallen into the trap of thinking that more detail equals more depth.
